CS-MU.name: Commercial Shopping Center-Mixed Use (CS-MU)

residential_allowed.assumption: Multi-family homes as part of a mixed-use shopping center.

approval.assumption: §9343 needs a conditional use permit, which we assume is granted in the home count.

lot_area_per_unit_sqft.assumption: At most 15 homes per acre: 43,560 divided by 15.

small_lot_units.assumption: A lot too small for one home keeps one home (assumed).

side_ft.assumption: None; 20 ft next to a residential district, not modeled.

rear_ft.assumption: Equal to the tallest building; we use the 35 ft limit.

max_stories.assumption: The code limits height to 35 ft, not stories; we fit 2 (conservative).

parking_per_unit.assumption: Homes follow the apartment table. One bedroom and up, condominiums and townhouses need 2.5 spaces (2 or 1.5 covered plus guest spaces); studios need 1.5. We use 2.5. None within ½ mile of a major transit stop (the AB 2097 path).

simplifications: §9344.1 sets a 5-acre minimum project site and §9343 needs a conditional use permit and commercial uses on the site. We don't model assembling lots; each lot is counted on its own, so small lots can run high.
20% to 33% of the floor area must be commercial; we count all of it as homes up to the density, which can run high.

residential_allowed.assumption: §9490.2 allows only parks, trails, wildlife preserves and passive recreation.

OS-R.name: Open Space-Restricted (OS-R)

residential_allowed.assumption: One home per lot, and only with a conditional use permit (§§9482, 9483). §9484 also allows an ADU once that permit is granted.

approval.assumption: One home, only with a conditional use permit (§§9482, 9483).

max_stories.assumption: The code limits height to 35 ft, not stories; we fit 2 (conservative).

sb9_allowed.assumption: SB 9 covers single-family residential zones. This is an open space district where a home needs a conditional use permit, so we don't apply SB 9 (conservative).

simplifications: The minimum lot and these standards are subject to the hillside rules (§9652), and we have no slope data, so hilly lots can run high. §9489.2 adds findings on habitat and hazards that can't be modeled.

RH.name: Residential, High Density (RH)

lot_area_per_unit_sqft.assumption: SCAG drops the number after the zone letters, so we use the lowest density of the range, RH-15 (2,400 sq ft per home); lots zoned higher run low.

small_lot_units.assumption: A lot too small for one home keeps one home (assumed).

parking_per_unit.assumption: One bedroom and up, condominiums and townhouses need 2.5 spaces (2 or 1.5 covered plus guest spaces); studios need 1.5. We use 2.5. None within ½ mile of a major transit stop (the AB 2097 path).

simplifications: Lots over 10% average slope follow the hillside rules (§9652), and we have no slope data, so hilly lots can run high.
300 sq ft of group open space per home is not modeled.

RL.name: Residential, Low Density (RL)

max_units_per_lot.assumption: One home per lot. The zone's density and minimum lot govern subdividing. State law (ADU, SB 9, Ch. 2 Part 11) is modeled separately.

side_ft.assumption: At least 12 ft per side, or 1/2 ft per foot of height; 15 ft at 30 ft of height is not modeled.

simplifications: Parking (2 covered spaces, §9654.2) isn't modeled; the one-home limit binds. Lots over 10% average slope follow the hillside rules (§9652), and we have no slope data.
The 35% site coverage also counts driveways and patios; the front yard grows with height, not modeled.

RM.name: Residential, Medium Density (RM)

approval.assumption: Apartment houses need a conditional use permit (§9252.4); other homes weren't confirmed.

lot_area_per_unit_sqft.assumption: SCAG drops the number after the zone letters, so we use the lowest density of the range, RM-6 (6,000 sq ft per home); lots zoned higher run low.

small_lot_units.assumption: A lot too small for one home keeps one home (assumed).

parking_per_unit.assumption: One bedroom and up, condominiums and townhouses need 2.5 spaces (2 or 1.5 covered plus guest spaces); studios need 1.5. We use 2.5. None within ½ mile of a major transit stop (the AB 2097 path).

simplifications: Apartment houses need a conditional use permit (§9252.4); other homes don't. Lots over 10% average slope follow the hillside rules (§9652), and we have no slope data, so hilly lots can run high.
250 sq ft of group open space per home is not modeled. The Affordable Housing overlay (20 to 25 per acre on RM-15 sites) isn't in our data.

RS.name: Residential, Single-Family (RS)

approval.assumption: One single-family dwelling per lot is a permitted use.

min_lot_area_sqft.assumption: The smallest of the range (RS-6-6,000); SCAG drops the suffix.

max_units_per_lot.assumption: One home per lot. The zone's density and minimum lot govern subdividing. State law (ADU, SB 9, Ch. 2 Part 11) is modeled separately.

side_ft.assumption: Lots under 10,000 sq ft: 18 ft combined, at least 8 ft on one side; we use 9 ft each. Larger lots use 22 ft combined and 25 ft front and rear, not modeled, so large lots can run high.

simplifications: Parking (2 covered spaces, §9654.2) isn't modeled; the one-home limit binds. Lots over 10% average slope follow the hillside rules (§9652), and we have no slope data.
SCAG drops the density and lot size after RS (RS-2-15,000 through RS-6-6,000).

RV.name: Residential, Very Low Density (RV)

max_units_per_lot.assumption: One home per lot. The zone's density and minimum lot govern subdividing. State law (ADU, SB 9, Ch. 2 Part 11) is modeled separately.

simplifications: Parking (2 covered spaces, §9654.2) isn't modeled; the one-home limit binds. Lots over 10% average slope follow the hillside rules (§9652), and we have no slope data.
The 25% site coverage also counts driveways and patios, so the buildable area can be smaller.

laws.name: Accessory Dwelling Units and Junior ADUs
laws.summary: On a lot with (or proposed for) one single-family home, the state allows one ADU plus one junior ADU (inside the house), whatever local density says. Pasadena allows ADUs in all residential zones and in CO/CL (PMC Tables 2-2 and 2-5, §17.50.275).

citation.section: Cal. Gov. Code §§66314-66342 (recodified from §65852.2 by SB 477, effective 2025)

assumptions: Applied wherever local zoning fits at least one home: the owner may build a house plus an ADU and a junior ADU instead of what local density allows. It's an alternative path (the larger of the two counts), not added on top.
Multifamily lots can also add ADUs under state law (conversions of non-living space and up to 8 detached ADUs, SB 1211). Not modeled yet, so multifamily ADU capacity is undercounted.

laws.name: SB 9 two-unit developments and urban lot splits
laws.summary: In single-family zones, the state allows two homes on a lot by right, and a one-time split of the lot into two, each allowed two homes: four in total. Pasadena adopted this as "Two-Unit Developments" (Table 2-2 note 5) and allows no ADUs on lots created by an urban lot split.

citation.section: Cal. Gov. Code §65852.21 (two-unit developments) and §66411.7 (urban lot splits)

assumptions: Each new lot must also be at least 40% of the original; splitting a lot in half always satisfies that, so we don't check it.

SB 9 doesn't apply where the work would demolish rent-restricted housing or housing rented in the last 3 years. We don't have tenancy data, so this is not checked; capacity on rented lots is overstated.
Lots in very high fire hazard zones can still use SB 9 if they meet fire mitigation standards, so they are not excluded.
The owner-occupancy affidavit required for lot splits is a condition of approval, not a capacity limit.
Lots under 1,200 sq ft get no SB 9 units (they are almost all strips and slivers, not house lots).

laws.name: AB 2097 no parking minimums near major transit
laws.summary: Cities may not require any minimum parking for housing within ½ mile of a major transit stop (Public Resources Code §21064.3).
assumptions: Distance is measured from the nearest edge of the lot, i.e. a lot counts if any part of it is within ½ mile. Measuring from the lot's center would cover fewer lots.
Major transit stops come from SCAG's 2022 base-year inventory, which uses the AB 2553 definition (20-minute peak headways).

laws.name: SB 79 transit-oriented development (2025)
laws.summary: Near qualifying stops, cities can't hold projects of 5 or more homes below set heights, densities and floor area. Tier 1 (heavy rail): 75 ft, 120 homes per acre and FAR 3.5 within a quarter mile, then 65 ft, 100 and 3. Tier 2 (light rail, qualifying bus): 65 ft, 100 and 3, then 55 ft, 80 and 2.5. Sites within 200 ft get +20 ft, +40 homes per acre and +1 FAR. Applies from July 1, 2026. We report it apart from base capacity, in a separate row.
assumptions: Stops, tiers and half-mile zones come from SCAG's official SB 79 map. Where SCAG shows the commuter rail tier two ways, we use its SB79_TIER field.
Local delay ordinances and alternative plans, including the City of LA's phased ordinance, aren't modeled, so a lot's number may not apply yet.
Tenant history, rent-controlled demolition limits, airport and fire rules aren't checked.
Above 10 homes, a project needs 7% extremely low, 10% very low or 13% lower income homes. Average home size can't exceed 1,750 sq ft.
Floor area becomes homes using the same gross sq ft per home as the rest of the engine.

laws.name: State Density Bonus Law
laws.summary: Projects with affordable homes can exceed local density. The largest mixed-income bonus is 50%, at 24% lower income or 15% very low income homes. A 100% affordable project gets 80%, with no density limit within a half mile of a major transit stop. We report these in separate rows.
assumptions: The percentage tables come from a law firm's 2022 chart (Meyers Nave), because the state's site couldn't be read. AB 1287's extra stacked bonus for added moderate income homes isn't modeled, so numbers can run low.
The bonus needs a numeric base density of at least 5 homes, so zones limited only by floor area show no number.
Waivers can lift physical limits, so these rows ignore yards, height and parking. Each is an upper estimate.
